title: React Internals Core Check
description: Check your understanding of React architecture, Fiber, reconciliation, render and commit phases, concurrent rendering, scheduling, batching, and Strict Mode.
author: DailyCoder

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes React's declarative model?

options.text: You describe the UI for a given state, and React figures out the DOM updates
You manually mutate every DOM node yourself
React stores CSS in the browser kernel
Components must always be classes

questions.explanation: React lets you describe what the UI should look like, then it reconciles and commits necessary updates.

questions.prompt: What is a Fiber in React's implementation?

options.text: A unit of work representing part of the component tree
A CSS file imported by a component
A browser-only network request
A replacement for JavaScript promises

questions.explanation: Fiber is React's internal structure for tracking component work, state, effects, and scheduling.

questions.prompt: During reconciliation, why do keys matter for lists?

options.text: They help React match children and preserve the right state across reorders
They make arrays sort alphabetically
They disable rerenders
They become CSS ids automatically

questions.explanation: Stable keys help React understand item identity, which is crucial for correct state preservation.

questions.prompt: What should happen during the render phase?

options.text: Pure calculation of the next UI
Direct DOM mutations and subscriptions
Synchronous localStorage writes on every render
Manual network retries

questions.explanation: Render should be pure. Side effects belong in effects, event handlers, or the commit phase mechanisms React controls.

questions.prompt: What happens in the commit phase?

options.text: React applies changes to the host environment and runs commit-related lifecycles and effects
React only compares JavaScript objects forever
React parses TypeScript types
React downloads npm packages

questions.explanation: The commit phase is when calculated changes are applied, refs update, layout effects run, and later passive effects are scheduled.

questions.prompt: Concurrent rendering means React may start rendering work, pause it, and continue or discard it before commit.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Concurrent rendering lets React interrupt and prioritize render work, but only committed work affects the DOM.

questions.prompt: Which ideas are related to batching and scheduling? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Multiple state updates can be grouped into one render
Updates can have different priorities
State updates are requests, not immediate variable mutations
Every `setState` always commits synchronously

questions.explanation: React can batch updates and schedule work by priority. State setters request updates rather than changing current render variables immediately.

questions.prompt: Why does Strict Mode intentionally double-invoke some development-only behavior?

options.text: To surface impure render logic and missing cleanup problems
To make production twice as slow
To prevent all effects from running
To replace testing libraries

questions.explanation: Strict Mode helps reveal side effects and cleanup issues during development. It does not double-invoke production behavior the same way.
